name: Salón París
subcategory: Neighborhood cantina with José Alfredo Jiménez lore
description: Family-friendly neighborhood cantina on Jaime Torres Bodet, with domino tables, the original wooden bar and Eiffel Tower paintings. Founded in the 1930s (sources say 1934 or 1939); a plaque marks the cantina where José Alfredo Jiménez began his career. Time Out praises the shrimp broth and carnitas; botana comes free with three drinks.
special_quality: The cantina where José Alfredo Jiménez started singing, still serving botana with every round.
address: Jaime Torres Bodet 152, Santa María la Ribera
google_maps_query: Salón París, Santa María la Ribera, Ciudad de Mexico

name: La Única de Guerrero
description: Opened 11 December 1933 on Guerrero street, beginning as a tiny five-square-metre room and growing into cantina, family restaurant and dance hall. Original folkloric decor and wooden bar have been kept for 80+ years and it has appeared on film. Specialty is oven-roasted cabrito.
special_quality: Eighty-plus years of unchanged decor in Colonia Guerrero, known for cabrito al horno and film cameos.
google_maps_query: La Única de Guerrero, Buenavista, Ciudad de Mexico

name: La Peninsular
description: Founded 1872 and often cited as the oldest cantina still operating in the Centro Histórico; remodeled in 2013 but retains vintage advertisements and a TV-sports feel. Sits on the pedestrian Alhóndiga street near La Merced.
special_quality: Claimed oldest working cantina in the historic center, serving since 1872.
google_maps_query: La Peninsular, Centro Histórico, Ciudad de Mexico

name: El Gallo de Oro
description: Dating to 1874 per guides, a somewhat gloomy corner cantina on Violeta and Carranza, recognized by a historian cited in El Economista as the successor in age to the lost El Nivel. Known for a Saturday cazuelas buffet.
special_quality: One of the oldest cantinas left standing after El Nivel, famed for Saturday cazuelas.
address: Violeta 1 esq. Venustiano Carranza, Centro Histórico
google_maps_query: El Gallo de Oro, Centro Histórico, Ciudad de Mexico

name: Tío Pepe
description: Opened around 1890 at Dolores and Independencia with many original fixtures, including a trough once used as a urinal at the base of the bar and beer-barrel lampshades. The old sign once barred women, minors and vendors; all are welcome now. Short menu, strong period atmosphere.
special_quality: Original 1890s fittings, down to the old bar-foot trough and the sign that once banned women.

name: La Potosina
description: Dates to 1890 on Pino Suárez, lively and busy, with a Santa Muerte statue out front and generous snack portions served with each drink. Legend (unverified) holds that Pancho Villa and Che Guevara drank there.
special_quality: Generous botanas with each drink in a cantina operating since 1890.
address: José María Pino Suárez 27, Centro Histórico
google_maps_query: La Potosina, Centro Histórico, Ciudad de Mexico

name: Bar La Ópera
description: Opened 1876 as a French bakery and operated as a cantina from 1906 to 1980; now more restaurant than drinking hall. Ornate Porfirian interior with a ceiling bullet hole attributed to Pancho Villa; Díaz, Fuentes and Paz are cited as patrons.
special_quality: The ceiling bullet hole and the gilded Porfirian room, a literary-political landmark.

name: La Faena
description: Large cantina on Carranza next to Bar Mancera, doubling as a bullfighting museum with matador suits and vintage posters. Good tequila, generous botanas and occasional mariachi.
special_quality: A cantina that is also a taurine museum, wall to wall in matador costumes.

name: Bar Mancera
description: Originally the bar of the Hotel Mancera, opened 1912 per a dpa piece cited by Time Out, with an elegant French-style air. Sits one door from La Faena.
special_quality: Most refined of the old Centro cantinas, born as a hotel bar in 1912.

name: El León de Oro
description: Established in 1954 in Colonia Escandón with live trios and traditional botanas, a multigenerational gathering place.

name: Cantina El Centenario
description: Tiny-changing cantina since 1948 on Vicente Suárez with bull's head, bullfighting posters, dominoes and tortilla española. Draws both older regulars and younger Condesa crowd.
special_quality: A 1948 cantina that has barely changed amid Condesa gentrification.

name: Cantina La Castellana
description: Opened as a grocery in 1892 and became a cantina in 1914, in San Rafael. Offers a buffet unlocked by drink spend (about $450 pesos per Mexico News Daily; Chilango cites a lower threshold).
special_quality: Buffet botana earned by drink spend in a 1914 San Rafael cantina.

name: Pulquería La Risa
description: Opened 1903 on Mesones and serves only pulque: natural, oat, nescafé, pineapple, strawberry with cream, piñón, tomato. Simple room with metal tables, vats and old photos.
special_quality: Pulque-only since 1903, plain and unreconstructed.
google_maps_query: Pulquería La Risa, Centro Histórico, Ciudad de Mexico

source_links.title: ADN40 — pulquerías más antiguas del Centro

name: Pulquería La Antigua Roma
description: More than 100 years old, serving Tlaxcala pulque with jukebox, renewed murals and the remnant of the old Departamento de Damas wall. Chicharrones and popcorn as botana; reopened after closing during the pandemic.
special_quality: Preserves the old women's-department wall, still serving natural pulque to regulars.
google_maps_query: Pulquería La Antigua Roma, Lagunilla, Ciudad de Mexico

source_links.title: ADN40 — pulquerías más antiguas del Centro

name: La Hija de los Apaches
subcategory: Pulquería run by a former boxer
description: About 70 years old, run by a former pro boxer whose photos cover the walls. Baticurado and bicentenario on Friday/Saturday, jukebox for 10 pesos, live salsa Wednesdays and rock on Fridays.
special_quality: Ex-boxer owner, secret-recipe curados and live music in Doctores.
google_maps_query: La Hija de los Apaches, Doctores, Ciudad de Mexico

source_links.title: ADN40 — pulquerías más antiguas del Centro

name: Pulquería La Victoria
description: Over 80 years old, run by the Ponce family since 2009. Famed for an ostión curado served only on Mondays from a family recipe; also guayaba, piñón, nuez and strawberry with cream.
special_quality: Monday-only oyster curado from a family recipe.
google_maps_query: Pulquería La Victoria, Aragón La Villa, Ciudad de Mexico

name: Pulquería La Hermosa Hortensia
description: Founded 1936 (one source says 1939) at the back of Plaza Garibaldi on Callejón de la Amargura. Murals and antiques, pulque only, curados from pineapple to chocolate, coffee and peanut. Touristy but a safe entry point.
special_quality: A pulque-only room among the mariachi bars with chocolate and peanut curados.
address: Callejón de la Amargura 4, Plaza Garibaldi
google_maps_query: Pulquería La Hermosa Hortensia, Plaza Garibaldi, Ciudad de Mexico

name: Pulquería La Nuclear
description: Roma pulquería mixing tradition and bar culture: mango, tuna, durazno, guayaba curados, a Friday huelia of pulque, amaranth, walnut, honey and almond. Also mezcal and sotol creams, weekend karaoke, popcorn on arrival.
special_quality: Friday huelia of pulque with amaranth and nuts, plus weekend karaoke.
google_maps_query: Pulquería La Nuclear, Roma Norte, Ciudad de Mexico

name: Pulquería La Pirata
description: Over 70 years old, serving only pulque by the liter, with takeout. Older regulars, a bolero shoe-shiner and banda on the jukebox; time-capsule feel.
special_quality: Time-capsule pulquería with a resident shoe shiner.
google_maps_query: Pulquería La Pirata, Escandón, Ciudad de Mexico

name: Pulquería La Bonita
description: About 101 years old per source, with boxing photos, bullfighting motifs and albur signs; celery and tomato curados, marzipan and piñón. Antojitos like salsa borracha with nopales.
special_quality: Albur signs, boxing photos and a celery pulque in a century-old room.
google_maps_query: Pulquería La Bonita, Nicolás Bravo, Ciudad de Mexico

name: Panana Pulquería
subcategory: Pulquería beneath the Museo del Pulque
description: Working pulquería in the ex-convent of San Hipólito serving pulque from Hidalgo, Tlaxcala and Edomex, with mixiotes, barbacoa and guacamole; the Museo del Pulque y las Pulquerías is upstairs.
special_quality: Pulquería under the city's pulque museum.
google_maps_query: Panana Pulquería, Centro Histórico, Ciudad de Mexico

name: Salón Covadonga
description: Spanish-style social club cantina on Puebla with domino regulars and, since the early 2000s, writers, artists and hipsters; menu leans to Spanish tortillas and tapas. Founded around 1940 per Mexico News Daily.
special_quality: Spanish émigré club turned cantina, shared by domino regulars and artists.
google_maps_query: Salón Covadonga, Roma Norte, Ciudad de Mexico

source_links.title: Mexico News Daily — Mexico City's best cantinas

name: La Jalisciense
description: Claimed 1870 founding, mahogany bar, wooden tables and historical photos in far north GAM; paella served Fridays.
special_quality: Friday paella in a mahogany-bar cantina dated to 1870.
google_maps_query: La Jalisciense, San Bartolo Atepehuacán, Ciudad de Mexico
